_comment: Differential Diagnosis Tree — chest pain workup leading to inferior STEMI vs. PE.
title: 🔍 Acute chest pain in a 52-year-old
caseHeader:
Chief complaint: 52-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden substernal chest pain that started 45 minutes ago, radiating to the left jaw.

Vitals: BP 138/86, HR 102, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, T 37.0°C. Diaphoretic, mildly anxious.

nodes.presentation: You are the on-call resident. Which investigation do you order first?

choices.addsToCase: ECG: 2 mm ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF; reciprocal depression in I and aVL.
choices.feedback: Good call — ECG within 10 minutes is standard for any chest pain consistent with ACS.

choices.addsToCase: CT-PA: no filling defects, normal lung parenchyma, incidental small pericardial effusion.
choices.feedback: Defensible if you suspect PE, but you're skipping the cheaper, faster first step.
An elevated D-dimer is non-specific in this clinical setting and won't rule in or out MI.

nodes.presentation: The ECG shows ST elevation in the inferior leads with reciprocal changes. Troponin is pending. What is your working diagnosis?

choices.text: Inferior STEMI — activate the cath lab
Acute pericarditis — start NSAIDs and observe

nodes.presentation: The CT-PA is negative for PE. The patient still has ongoing pain and an unexplained tachycardia. What do you order next?

choices.addsToCase: ECG (delayed by ~30 min): 2 mm ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes.

nodes.presentation: The elevated D-dimer doesn't help discriminate. The patient's pain is worsening. What do you do?

choices.addsToCase: ECG (after D-dimer): 2 mm ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes.

diagnosis.name: Inferior STEMI
diagnosis.explanation: Correct. ST elevation in II, III, and aVF with reciprocal changes is diagnostic of an inferior wall STEMI — most often a right coronary artery occlusion. Door-to-balloon time should be under 90 minutes.

diagnosis.name: Acute pericarditis
diagnosis.explanation: Incorrect. Pericarditis classically causes diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, not a focal inferior pattern with reciprocal changes. Treating this as pericarditis would delay reperfusion in an evolving STEMI.

diagnosis.name: Pulmonary embolism
diagnosis.explanation: Incorrect. PE can cause sinus tachycardia and right-heart strain on ECG (S1Q3T3), but it does not produce focal inferior ST elevation with reciprocal depression. Anticoagulation without revascularization would miss the STEMI.
